claim: Infections with low or undetected blood parasites are common in Human African Trypanosomiasis caused by Trypanosoma brucei gambiense.
source: Intriguingly, infections with low or undetected blood parasites are common, particularly in the case of Human African Trypanosomiasis caused by Trypanosoma brucei gambiense.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on asymptomatic individuals and long-term seropositives mentioned later in the introduction.

claim: Substantial quantities of trypanosomes exist within the skin following experimental infection.
source: Here we definitively show that substantial quantities of trypanosomes exist within the skin following experimental infection, which can be transmitted to the tsetse vector, even in the absence of detectable parasitaemia.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including histological analysis, bioluminescence imaging, and xenodiagnosis experiments.

claim: Skin trypanosomes can be transmitted to the tsetse vector even in the absence of detectable parasitaemia.
source: Here we definitively show that substantial quantities of trypanosomes exist within the skin following experimental infection, which can be transmitted to the tsetse vector, even in the absence of detectable parasitaemia.
evidence: This claim is supported by xenodiagnosis experiments showing tsetse infection from skin parasites in mice with undetectable blood parasitaemia.

claim: Extravascular parasites are present in human skin biopsies from undiagnosed individuals.
source: Importantly, we demonstrate the presence of extravascular parasites in human skin biopsies from undiagnosed individuals.
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopic examination of historical human skin biopsies from the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

claim: Asymptomatic individuals can represent a significant proportion of the infected population in vector-borne diseases.
source: In a number of vector-borne diseases, it is becoming evident that asymptomatic individuals, be they humans or animals, can represent a significant proportion of the infected population and therefore an important reservoir of disease that requires targeting by control measures (Lindblade et al., 2014; Fakhar, 2013; Koffi et al., 2006; Berthier et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on asymptomatic infections in vector-borne diseases.

claim: Asymptomatic individuals with human trypanosomiasis (long-term seropositives) but undetected parasitaemia have been identified in West Africa.
source: The recent identification in West Africa of asymptomatic individuals with human trypanosomiasis (long-term seropositives) but undetected parasitaemia, raises the question of what role these individuals play in disease transmission (Koffi et al., 2006; Jamonneau et al., 2012; Bucheton et al., 2011; Kanmogne et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research identifying asymptomatic individuals in West Africa.

claim: Therapy for trypanosomiasis is currently only directed towards microscopy-positive individuals.
source: Therapy is currently only directed towards microscopy-positive individuals and thus a proportion of the infected population remain untreated.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of current treatment policies for trypanosomiasis.

claim: Seropositive individuals with low or undetected parasitaemia contain transmissible trypanosomes.
source: There is convincing evidence that seropositive individuals with low or undetected parasitaemia contain transmissible trypanosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by xenodiagnosis experiments cited in the following sentences.

claim: Xenodiagnosis experiments have shown that tsetse flies fed on microscopy-negative infected humans became infected.
source: Xenodiagnosis experiments, in which tsetse flies are fed on microscopy-negative infected humans (Frezil, 1971) or, more recently, experimentally-infected pigs (Wombou Toukam et al., 2011), have shown that these apparently aparasitaemic hosts contain the parasite since the tsetse flies became infected.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to xenodiagnosis experiments in humans and pigs.

claim: Tsetse flies have a telmophagus (slash and suck) feeding habit.
source: It is uncertain where the trypanosomes reside in the host but, given the telmophagus (slash and suck) feeding habit of the tsetse fly, they could be skin-dwelling parasites ingested with the blood meal.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about tsetse fly feeding behavior.

claim: Cutaneous symptoms and distinct 'trypanid' skin lesions are associated with African trypanosomiasis.
source: Detection of trypanosomes in the skin is not well documented, although there are descriptions of cutaneous symptoms associated with African trypanosomiasis and distinct 'trypanid' skin lesions (McGovern et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on cutaneous symptoms.

claim: Imaging data from mouse models suggest that trypanosomes sequester to major organs such as the spleen, liver and brain.
source: Imaging data from mouse models of infection suggest that trypanosomes sequester to major organs such as the spleen, liver and brain (Blum et al., 2008; Kennedy, 2004) and recent evidence has demonstrated trypanosomes in extravascular adipose tissue (Trindade et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior imaging studies in mouse models.

claim: Trypanosomes have been demonstrated in extravascular adipose tissue.
source: Imaging data from mouse models of infection suggest that trypanosomes sequester to major organs such as the spleen, liver and brain (Blum et al., 2008; Kennedy, 2004) and recent evidence has demonstrated trypanosomes in extravascular adipose tissue (Trindade et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent research on adipose-associated trypanosomes.

claim: Adipose-associated trypanosomes appear to be a new life-cycle stage with a distinct transcriptional profile.
source: These adipose-associated trypanosomes appear to be a new life-cycle stage with a distinct transcriptional profile and, while tsetse bite-site associated transmission has been suggested (Caljon et al., 2016), and a historical study made a passing observation of localised deposition of trypanosomes in the skin matrix (Goodwin, 1971), the broader role of skin-dwelling trypanosomes in transmission remains unclear.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cited research on adipose-associated trypanosomes.

claim: T.b. brucei and T.b. gambiense invade the extravascular tissue of the skin including but not restricted to the adipose tissue.
source: We provide conclusive evidence of T.b. brucei, (a causative agent of animal trypanosomiasis) and the human-infective trypanosome, T.b. gambiense, invading the extravascular tissue of the skin (including but not restricted to the adipose tissue) and undergoing onward transmission despite undetected vascular parasitaemia.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological and imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Skin trypanosomes undergo onward transmission despite undetected vascular parasitaemia.
source: We provide conclusive evidence of T.b. brucei, (a causative agent of animal trypanosomiasis) and the human-infective trypanosome, T.b. gambiense, invading the extravascular tissue of the skin (including but not restricted to the adipose tissue) and undergoing onward transmission despite undetected vascular parasitaemia.
evidence: This claim is supported by xenodiagnosis experiments showing tsetse infection from skin parasites in mice without detectable blood parasitaemia.

claim: Trypanosomes localize within the skin of undiagnosed humans.
source: We also provide evidence of localisation of trypanosomes within the skin of undiagnosed humans.
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopic examination of historical human skin biopsies.

claim: Extravascular parasites were first observed in the skin 12 days post-infection in BALB/c mice infected with T. brucei STIB247.
source: Extravascular parasites were first observed in the skin 12 days post-infection and remained throughout the experiment.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis data from the time-course experiment.

claim: Skin parasite numbers fluctuated to a lesser extent than blood parasitaemia in BALB/c mice infected with T. brucei STIB247.
source: Skin parasite numbers fluctuated to a lesser extent than blood parasitaemia and the apparent periodicity in the skin may be due to one particularly high data point on day 24 (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of blood parasitaemia and skin parasite burden data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Parasites were found in the dermis, subcutaneous adipose tissue and in fascia beneath the panniculus carnosus muscle.
source: Parasites were found in the dermis, subcutaneous adipose tissue (Figure 2) and in fascia beneath the panniculus carnosus muscle.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The presence of parasites in the skin was not associated with major inflammation in BALB/c mice infected with T. brucei STIB247.
source: The presence of parasites in the skin was not associated with major inflammation (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by histopathological assessment data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The more virulent TREU927 strain of T. brucei and the human-infective T.b. gambiense strain PA showed extravascular skin invasion of the dermis, subcutaneous adipose tissue and fascial planes.
source: To confirm that skin invasion by this parasite was not strain or sub-species specific, the more virulent TREU927 strain of T. brucei and the human-infective T.b. gambiense strain, PA, were used to infect mice. Extravascular skin invasion of the dermis, subcutaneous adipose tissue and fascial planes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) was evident with associated mild to moderate inflammation (Supplementary file 2), in some instances the degree of skin invasion in the T.b. gambiense infected mice was far greater than T.b. brucei, perhaps suggesting a greater propensity for sequestration in this sub-species.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: T.b. gambiense may have a greater propensity for skin sequestration than T.b. brucei.
source: in some instances the degree of skin invasion in the T.b. gambiense infected mice was far greater than T.b. brucei, perhaps suggesting a greater propensity for sequestration in this sub-species.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on observations of greater skin invasion in some T.b. gambiense infected mice.

claim: Parasites were observed in the skin following natural vector transmission by a single infective bite of G.m. morsitans.
source: Mice were infected by a single infective bite of an individual G.m. morsitans. After 4 to 11 days and up to the end of the experiment, parasites were observed in the skin with a dynamic distribution (Figure 3A) and a variable density (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioluminescence imaging data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Parasites were first detected in the blood between 5 and 19 days after natural transmission in mice infected by tsetse bite.
source: Parasites were first detected in the blood between 5 and 19 days after natural transmission and parasitaemia remained lower than 10 (Kanmogne et al., 1996) parasites/ml.
evidence: This claim is supported by parasitaemia monitoring data from naturally infected mice.

claim: Bioluminescence directly reflects the total number of living parasites in the entire organism, including blood and viscera.
source: Observed bioluminescence directly reflects the total number of living parasites in the entire organism, including blood and viscera, but the intensity of the signal decreases with tissue depth.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of bioluminescence imaging principles.

claim: In addition to the skin, only the spleen, some lymph nodes and adipose tissue were observed to be positive for bioluminescence in several individuals after natural transmission.
source: In addition to the skin, only the spleen, some lymph nodes and adipose tissue were observed to be positive for bioluminescence in several individuals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioluminescence imaging of dissected organs shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The observed bioluminescence is likely to originate predominantly, but not solely, from parasites in the skin.
source: This suggests that the observed bioluminescence is likely to originate predominantly, but not solely, from parasites in the skin.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that few organs other than skin showed bioluminescence.

claim: Only mild inflammation was observed after 29 days in mice infected by natural transmission.
source: In addition, only mild inflammation was observed after 29 days (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by histopathological analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Extravascular trypanosomes observed in the dermal layer of dorsal skin were highly motile.
source: Extravascular trypanosomes observed in the dermal layer of dorsal skin were highly motile, consistent with viability (Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by 2-photon microscopy imaging shown in Video 1.

claim: Extravascular trypanosomes were observed in the dermal layer of the ear and were highly motile in C57BL/6J-Flk1-EGFP mice.
source: Extravascular trypanosomes were observed in the dermal layer of the ear and were highly motile (Videos 2, 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by spinning-disk confocal microscopy imaging shown in Videos 2, 3, and 4.

claim: Approximately 20% of skin-dwelling parasites were stumpy forms based on PAD1/ZFP3 transcript abundance.
source: Using the relative transcript abundance of the stumpy marker Protein Associated with Differentiation 1 (PAD1) (Dean et al., 2009) to an endogenous control, Zinc Finger Protein 3 (ZFP3) (Walrad et al., 2009), we estimated that approximately 20% of skin-dwelling parasites were stumpy (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data on PAD1/ZFP3 relative expression in Supplementary file 3.

claim: PAD1-positive cells were observed in variable proportions (from 8 to 80%) in all bioluminescent skin samples examined after IP injection.
source: PAD1-positive cells were observed in variable proportions (from 8 to 80%) in all bioluminescent skin samples examined after IP injection (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence analysis data in Supplementary file 4.

claim: Up to 38% of parasites detected using VSG surface markers also expressed PAD1 following natural transmission.
source: Following natural transmission, up to 38% of parasites detected using VSG surface markers (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–B) also expressed PAD1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C–D) (n = 441 cells from 8 skin sections).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Stumpy parasites were homogenously distributed in the dermis and subcutaneous adipose tissues in all skin sections.
source: In all skin sections, stumpy parasites were homogenously distributed in the dermis and subcutaneous adipose tissues.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological observations of PAD1-positive cells in skin sections.

claim: In mice with undetectable or low parasitaemia (<5 × 10^4 parasites/ml), no parasites were found in flies fed on non-bioluminescent regions.
source: In mice with undetectable or low parasitaemia (<5 × 104 parasites/ml), no parasites were found in flies fed on non-bioluminescent regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by xenodiagnosis experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: A median of 36% (± 23%, n = 70) of flies that fed on bioluminescent regions of low parasitaemic mice became infected.
source: Conversely, a median of 36% (± 23%, n = 70) of flies that fed on bioluminescent regions of low parasitaemic mice became infected (Table 1 and Table 1—source data 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by xenodiagnosis experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Skin parasites from mice without visible parasitaemia can contribute to tsetse infection.
source: This demonstrates that skin parasites, from mice without visible parasitaemia, can contribute to tsetse infection, possibly reflecting human asymptomatic infections.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the xenodiagnosis data showing tsetse infection from skin parasites in low parasitaemic mice.

claim: When parasites were detected in the blood and skin, tsetse infection rates increased up to 100% (median of 61% ± 22%, n = 120).
source: When parasites were detected in the blood and skin, tsetse infection rates increased up to 100% (median of 61% ± 22%, n = 120) (Table 1 and Table 1—source data 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by xenodiagnosis experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Parasites taken-up from the skin were able to further develop through the life-cycle to early procyclic forms in the fly.
source: Parasites taken-up from the skin were able to further develop through the life-cycle to early procyclic forms in the fly as evidenced by GPEET-procyclin marker on the parasites surface (n = 721 cells from 16 flies) (Table 1—source data 4 and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence analysis of parasites in tsetse midguts.

claim: Re-examination of 1121 skin biopsies by microscopy revealed six individuals with trypanosomes in their skin.
source: Re-examination of 1121 skin biopsies by microscopy revealed six individuals with trypanosomes in their skin (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopic examination of historical human skin biopsies shown in Figure 5.

claim: The six individuals with trypanosomes in their skin had not previously been diagnosed with human trypanosomiasis by clinical signs or the presence of blood parasites.
source: These individuals had not previously been diagnosed with human trypanosomiasis by clinical signs or the presence of blood parasites.
evidence: This claim is based on the historical records associated with the skin biopsy samples.

claim: There exists a significant yet overlooked population of live, motile, extravascular T. brucei in the dermis and subcutis of animal models infected by artificial routes or by vector transmission.
source: We have shown that there exists a significant yet overlooked population of live, motile, extravascular T. brucei in the dermis and subcutis of animal models infected by artificial routes or by vector transmission.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined histological, imaging, and intravital microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Skin parasites are ingested during tsetse fly pool-feeding and readily initiate cyclical development in the vector.
source: It is likely that once injected the parasites disseminate via the lymph and blood to the skin where they are ingested during tsetse fly pool-feeding and readily initiate cyclical development in the vector.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the xenodiagnosis data showing tsetse infection and development of procyclic forms from skin parasites.

claim: It is possible that more parasites exist in the skin than in the blood, depending on the density of skin invasion.
source: Given the relative volume of the skin organ compared to the vasculature, it is possible, depending on the density of skin invasion, that more parasites exist in the skin than in the blood.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the relative volumes of skin and blood and observed parasite densities.

claim: The skin represents an unappreciated reservoir of infection.
source: The skin, therefore, represents an unappreciated reservoir of infection.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing substantial skin parasite populations that can transmit to tsetse.

claim: Skin-dwelling trypanosomes contribute to transmission and could explain the maintenance of disease foci, despite active screening and treatment.
source: Here we show that these skin-dwelling trypanosomes contribute to transmission and could explain the maintenance of disease foci, despite active screening and treatment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the xenodiagnosis data and speculates on the epidemiological implications.

claim: Skin invasion for enhanced transmission is likely a powerful evolutionary force driving extravasation.
source: Skin invasion for enhanced transmission is likely a powerful evolutionary force driving extravasation, suggesting that the generalised tissue penetration underlying pathogenesis (i.e. splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, CNS invasion) is a secondary epiphenomenon.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing an evolutionary explanation for observed parasite behavior.

claim: A skin reservoir presents a novel target for diagnostics (e.g. skin biopsies).
source: A skin reservoir also presents a novel target for diagnostics (e.g. skin biopsies), allowing the prevalence of infection to be accurately determined and the identification of any previously undetected animal reservoirs of human disease.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing potential applications of the findings.

claim: The skin as an anatomical reservoir of parasites is a recurring theme in arthropod-borne human diseases such as Leishmania and Onchocerca.
source: The skin as an anatomical reservoir of parasites is a recurring theme in arthropod-borne human diseases such as Leishmania (Sacks, 2008; Schlein, 1993) and Onchocerca (Symptomatology, 1974; Dalmat, 1955).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on skin reservoirs in other parasitic diseases.

claim: The skin anatomical reservoir may explain how HAT foci re-emerge and persist despite low numbers of reported cases even in the absence of an animal reservoir.
source: This anatomical reservoir may serve to explain how HAT foci re-emerge and persist despite low numbers of reported cases even in the absence of an animal reservoir (Kagbadouno et al., 2012; Cordon-Obras et al., 2009; Balyeidhusa et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing an explanation for HAT epidemiology based on the skin reservoir findings.

claim: HAT was once widespread across much of sub-Saharan Africa but concerted control efforts brought it close to elimination during the 1960s.
source: HAT was once widespread across much of sub-Saharan Africa but concerted control efforts brought it close to elimination during the 1960s (World Health Organization 2000, 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on historical knowledge and WHO reports on HAT control.

claim: Disease foci persisted with a resurgence in the number of reported HAT cases to over 300,000 in the 1990s.
source: However, disease foci persisted, with a resurgence in the number of reported cases to over 300,000 in the 1990s (World Health Organization 2000; Steverding, 2008).
evidence: This claim is based on historical epidemiological data from WHO and other sources.

claim: HAT is currently approaching elimination in many areas.
source: Currently, HAT is approaching elimination in many areas (World Health Organization 2013; Simarro et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on recent WHO reports and epidemiological studies.

claim: It may be necessary to develop novel therapeutics capable of accessing extravascular compartments.
source: For example, our results indicate that it may be necessary to develop novel therapeutics capable of accessing extravascular compartments.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a therapeutic implication of the findings.

claim: The current policy in most endemic countries is not to treat serologically positive individuals unless they demonstrate active infection.
source: The current policy in most endemic countries is not to treat serologically positive individuals unless they demonstrate active infection, due to the long duration and high toxicity of treatment and the low predictive value of the serological tests.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of current HAT treatment policies.

claim: Serologically positive individuals represent a carrier population which may maintain HAT foci.
source: We suggest that this policy should be reconsidered in light of our compelling evidence that they represent a carrier population which may maintain HAT foci and explain previously thwarted efforts to eliminate this major pathogen.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data on skin parasites in asymptomatic individuals and speculates on epidemiological implications.

claim: STIB247 is a low virulence T.b. brucei strain that induces a chronic infection and was isolated from a hartebeest in the Serengeti in 1971.
source: STIB247 is a low virulence T.b. brucei strain that induces a chronic infection and was isolated from a hartebeest in the Serengeti in 1971 (Geigy et al., 1973).
evidence: This claim is based on citation to the original isolation and characterization of the strain.

claim: TREU927 is the genome reference strain for T. brucei and is more virulent than STIB247.
source: TREU927 is the genome reference strain for T. brucei and is more virulent than STIB247. This strain was isolated from a tsetse fly in Kenya in 1969/1970 (Goedbloed et al., 1973).
evidence: This claim is based on citation to the original isolation and established knowledge of TREU927 as the reference strain.

claim: PA is a human-infective group 1 T.b. gambiense strain isolated from a patient in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 1975.
source: PA is a human-infective group 1 T.b. gambiense strain isolated from a patient in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 1975 (Tait et al., 1984).
evidence: This claim is based on citation to the original isolation and characterization of the strain.

claim: The AnTat 1.1E clone of T.b. brucei was derived from a strain originally isolated from a bushbuck in Uganda in 1966.
source: The AnTat 1.1E clone of T.b. brucei was derived from a strain originally isolated from a bushbuck in Uganda in 1966 (Le Ray et al., 1977).
evidence: This claim is based on citation to the original isolation of the strain.

claim: Parasite density and bioluminescence intensity were correlated when bioluminescence levels were higher than 10^4 p/s/cm²/sr, corresponding to about 10^3 parasites.
source: Parasite density and bioluminescence intensity were correlated when bioluminescence levels were higher than 104 p/s/cm²/sr, corresponding to about 103 parasites, allowing estimation of the parasite density from in vivo imaging over this threshold (Table 1—source data 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by calibration experiments shown in Table 1—source data 1B.

claim: The incidence of trypanosomiasis was 1.5–2% at the time of skin biopsy sampling in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
source: At the time of sampling, the incidence of trypanosomiasis was 1.5–2% and we hypothesised that some individuals may have harboured undiagnosed infections.
evidence: This claim is based on historical epidemiological data from the sampling period.

claim: A clearly identifiable stumpy transmission form with typical morphology and an unattached undulating membrane is present in the skin of one individual.
source: In addition to visible slender forms (black arrows) in the extravascular tissue of the skin, a clearly identifiable stumpy transmission form with typical morphology and an unattached undulating membrane is also present in the skin of one individual (red arrow in A).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopic observation shown in Figure 5.
